article.title: Diversity, Equity & Inclusion
article.author: W. D. Ehrhart
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. During the first Trump administration, Donald Trump made clear his opposition to anything promoting Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI). Almost immediately after he was sworn in for a second time, Trump attacked DEI with a vengeance, issuing an executive order requiring federal agencies and contactors to disband DEI programs, and aggressively pursuing policies designed to erase any evidence that DEI or the fruits of DEI had ever existed. This included, but was hardly limited to, purging federal contractors, universities, and corporations of anything that smacked of DEI. Trump supporters at almost every level reflected this animosity, often arguing that DEI was really a way of disguising an aggressive LGBTQ+ agenda to corrupt American youth and turn them all into gays and lesbians while promoting and advantaging undeserving minorities. In 2022, in the community where I grew up, the Pennridge School Board disbanded its Diversity Equity Inclusion Committee, replacing it with an unwieldy ad hoc committee chaired by the then-board president, who had gone on record insisting that there was no such thing as structural or institutional racism in our community or the nation at large. Though the members of the school board have changed since then, to my knowledge the DEI Committee has never been resurrected. Related: All the News That’s Fit to Print? I would have to say, however, that this mid-term election has powerfully demonstrated the failure of attempts to erase diversity, equity, and inclusion (the use of lower case letters is deliberate) from the fabric of this country. A significant number of Americans seem to be quite comfortable with DEI. New Mexico, for instance, just elected a Native American governor, and a woman at that. Georgia elected a Black woman governor. Wisconsin, Nevada, and Florida just elected Black men as their governors, and the guy who won Florida is even a Republican. California elected its first Latino governor since 1875, and Texas elected a Latina woman to the governorship. Ohio gets a “twofer” with its first governor who is both a woman and Jewish. In various congressional races, Minnesota elected the first native American woman to the US senate while Michigan elected the first ever Muslim. The first openly gay senator will represent New Hampshire. Illinois makes history as the first state to be represented in the US senate by two women of color. And Mississippi has just elected a Black man for the first time since Reconstruction. Over in the House, both Indiana and Michigan will send their states’ first gay men to Washington. A bisexual woman has beaten the incumbent Republican in California while openly lesbian women have flipped Red seats in Arizona and New York. Related: What Rawand Dreams Of These amazing election results continue right on down the ballot. Michigan will have its first Black gay state senator and its first transgender legislator. Rhode Island elected an LGBTQ+ as attorney general, the first ever to win a statewide office. Alabama will have its first transgender state legislator while Georgia elected a transgender nonbinary person to its state legislature. If you have the time to look it all up, this just goes on and on and on from state legislatures to county commissioners to town councils. Clearly, a whole lot of voters actively embrace diversity, equity, and inclusion, and don’t mind being governed by people who do not happen to be straight white men. However, those of you who find all this diversity, equity, and inclusion a bit unnerving can rest assured that these United States have not yet been completely overrun by assorted minorities you may not be entirely comfortable with. There were 425 elections for the US House of Representatives, 35 more for the US Senate, 36 gubernatorial races, and hundreds and hundreds of races for various state legislatures. In Pennsylvania alone, there were 228 races on the ballot. Related: The Most Critical Profession on the Planet Two of the most watched races for the US House of Representatives in Pennsylvania, both of which flipped from Red to Blue, were won by heterosexual married white men. Two other key races in this state that also flipped from Red to Blue were won by heterosexual married white women. So I don’t think we’re in any danger of being governed solely by—what shall we call them—non-traditional persons of varying backgrounds with lifestyles different from what we are most comfortable with. But I have to admit that it sure is fun to see so many interesting candidates getting elected by Americans who just don’t feel threatened by people who are different from them. The president and his supporters notwithstanding, it seems that Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion are still as American as apple pie.
